sources.title: Quechuas

sources.title: The Expansion and Distribution of Quechua
sources.note: Academic linguistic synthesis showing that Quechuan expansion predates and cannot be reduced to Inca imperial expansion.

sources.title: Quechua

sources.title: Quechua language prehistory and Inca expansion
sources.note: PUCP archaeological-linguistic study separating older Quechuan dispersals from later Inca promotion.

sources.title: Quechua expansion during the Inca and colonial periods
sources.note: Cambridge account of imperial and colonial Quechua expansion, contact, and koineization.

sources.title: The Oxford Handbook of the Incas
sources.note: Academic synthesis of the multiethnic Inca Empire, imperial institutions, provincial agency, colonial change, and continuity.

sources.title: Inka Road History Timeline
sources.note: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian chronology of expansion, invasion, disease, civil war, and transformation.

sources.title: Central and Southern Andes, 1400 to 1600
sources.note: Metropolitan Museum chronology of rulers, expansion, provincial centers, invasion, and Vilcabamba.

sources.title: Inca Apocalypse
sources.note: Oxford study emphasizing decades of conquest and colonial transformation rather than an instant Andean ending at Cajamarca.

sources.title: History of how the Spaniards arrived in Peru
sources.note: Library of Congress description of Titu Cusi Yupanqui’s 1570 Indigenous account and its Quechua-Spanish mediation.

sources.title: Qhapaq Ñan, Andean Road System
sources.note: UNESCO account of the road network, shared infrastructure, storage, drainage, communication, and living guardianship.

sources.title: The Inka Empire and Q’eswachaka
sources.note: Smithsonian child-readable overview of Tawantinsuyu, reciprocity, roads, and continuing bridge renewal.

sources.title: Extending the Agricultural Area
sources.note: Smithsonian community interview on older terraces, Inca innovation, soils, irrigation, drainage, and continuity.

sources.title: Explore Water Management
sources.note: Smithsonian explanation of canals, springs, fountains, terraces, and water engineering at Inca sites.

sources.title: Inka Water Management Today
sources.note: Smithsonian interviews with local water experts about shared maintenance, irrigation, drinking water, and modern constraints.

sources.title: Food Diversification
sources.note: Smithsonian account of Andean ecological zones, potatoes, quinoa, maize, chuño, camelids, guinea pigs, and living farming.

sources.title: Ways of Living
sources.note: Smithsonian account of khipu, state storage, Guaman Poma images, farming seasons, and evidence limits.

sources.title: Khipu
sources.note: British Museum record for a dated Inca cotton khipu with cords, knots, and recorded archaeological context.

sources.title: Quipu 41-52-30/2863
sources.note: Harvard Peabody Museum object record documenting one khipu’s materials, colors, knots, and provenance.

sources.title: Inca tunic
sources.note: Met object record for a 1450 to 1550 highland camelid-fiber garment showing technical and regional connections.

sources.title: The Andean Tunic, 400 BCE to 1800 CE
sources.note: Met exhibition on gendered garments, materials, regional styles, storage, wear, and colonial continuities.

sources.title: Andean Textiles
sources.note: Met essay on weaving traditions, specialist female and male weavers, materials, color, and imperial workshops.

sources.title: Gender and Status in Inca Textile and Ceramic Craft Production
sources.note: Peer-reviewed chapter on gender, status, specialist craftspeople, widespread production, labor service, and state gifts.

sources.title: Hearths, Grinding Stones, and Households
sources.note: Archaeological study of households, kin support, women’s and men’s labor, children’s tasks, and limits of ayllu models.

sources.title: Landscapes of Pre-Hispanic Andean Kinship
sources.note: Academic review of ayllu as flexible kin, place, labor, ancestor, and land relations with debated antiquity.

sources.title: Cranial trepanation in pre-Columbian Peruvian cultures
sources.note: Medical-history review of trepanation across several Peruvian cultures and its continuation during Inca rule.

sources.title: Travel medicine, coca and cocaine
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of coca’s long Andean history, uses, and uncertain relationship to medical procedures.

sources.title: Sanitary and Ritual Meaning on Water Supply and Drainage System in Machu Picchu
sources.note: Engineering study of water supply and drainage at one elite Inca site, with sanitary and ritual interpretation.

sources.title: Water supply and drainage system in Pisac
sources.note: Field study of waterworks and health-risk management at one Inca site.

sources.title: The Guaman Poma Website
sources.note: Royal Danish Library facsimile, transcription, and scholarly apparatus for Guaman Poma’s 1615 or 1616 autograph manuscript.

sources.title: The Huarochiri Manuscript
sources.note: University of Texas Press account of a circa 1600 regional Quechua manuscript, its local tellers, text, and translation.

sources.title: The Huarochirí Manuscript
sources.note: Smithsonian Libraries record identifying the colonial-era Quechua narrative and its later transcription and translation.

sources.title: Resistance and Adaptation
sources.note: Smithsonian account of Indigenous resistance, textile continuity, adaptation, and colonial survival.

sources.title: Rijchariy intercultural health platform
sources.note: Peru Ministry of Health evidence for current Indigenous participation in intercultural health and knowledge governance.

sources.title: Oral traditions and expressions
sources.note: UNESCO guidance on oral knowledge, variation, transmission, community performers, and living safeguarding.
